concepts.en: Value of each digit in decimals
Round to the nearest whole number

summary.big_en: Every digit in a number has a value that depends on its place. Moving a digit one place changes its value ten times.

glossary.def: One of the symbols 0 to 9 that a number is written with.
glossary.example: The digit 7 in 213.807 stands for 7 thousandths (p.13).

glossary.def: The value a digit has because of its position in the number.
glossary.example: In 6703.46 the digit 7 has a place value of 7 hundreds (p.13).

glossary.def: The dot that separates the whole-number part from the part smaller than one.
glossary.example: In 13.136 the decimal point comes after the 13 (p.13).

glossary.def: A number written with a decimal point, so it can show parts smaller than one.
glossary.example: 0.375 inches is the wingspan of a Western Pygmy Blue Butterfly (p.12).

glossary.def: The first place after the decimal point, worth one tenth each.
The second place after the decimal point, worth one hundredth each.
The third place after the decimal point, worth one thousandth each.
Putting parts together to make a number.
Splitting a number into the parts it is made of.
Writing the same number as a different set of parts.
glossary.example: 56.079 regroups as 56 ones and 79 thousandths (WB p.9).

points.t: The value of a digit depends on its place, not on the digit itself. The 7 in 6703.46 is 7 hundreds; the 7 in 213.807 is 7 thousandths (p.13).
The three places after the decimal point are tenths, hundredths and thousandths (p.13).
Multiplying by 10, 100 or 1000 moves every digit 1, 2 or 3 places to the left. Dividing moves them the same number of places to the right (p.14).
Adding zeros is not the same as multiplying by 100. 5.6 × 100 is 560, not 5.600 (WB p.12).
The same number can be regrouped in many ways, and every way has the same total (p.13).

checklists.title: Places in 13.136 (p.13)
checklists.note: Reading a number aloud place by place is the quickest way to check a digit's value.

watch_out.wrong: I can multiply by 100 by adding two zeros.
watch_out.right: That only works for whole numbers: 5.6 × 100 is 560, because every digit moves two places left (WB p.12).

worked.title: Worked example 1 — write it as a decimal
worked.problem: Write 3 + 6 thousandths + 10 + 3 hundredths + 1 tenth as a decimal number.
steps: Write the terms in order of size, starting with the highest place value: 10 + 3 + 1 tenth + 3 hundredths + 6 thousandths.
Put each digit in its column on a place value grid: 1 ten, 3 ones, 1 tenth, 3 hundredths, 6 thousandths.
Read the grid straight off, keeping every column.
worked.why: Ordering by place value first means no digit ends up in the wrong column.

worked.title: Worked example 1 — reverse the operations
worked.problem: A number is divided by 10 and then by 100, and the answer is 0.375. What was the number?
steps: Dividing is undone by multiplying, so work backwards: 0.375 × 100 × 10.
× 100 × 10 is the same as × 1000, so every digit moves three places left.
worked.why: Reversing the operations turns a puzzle into one calculation.

summary.big_en: Rounding replaces a number with a nearby simpler one. Look at the digit just after the place you are rounding to.

glossary.def: Replace a number with a nearby number that is easier to use.
The closest of the possible answers.
One of the positions after the decimal point.
glossary.example: An answer rounded to the nearest tenth has one decimal place (p.16).

points.t: Rounding makes numbers easier to describe and understand. Saying a race took under 10 seconds is easier than 9.63 seconds (p.16).
The digit you look at is always the one just after the place you are rounding to (p.16).
An answer rounded to the nearest tenth always has one decimal place, even when it is zero (p.16).
To round to the nearest whole number, look at the tenths digit by the same rule (p.16).

checklists.title: Which way to round (p.16)

items.look_for: round down — keep the digit the same
round up — add 1 to the digit

checklists.note: The same rule works for any place; only the digit you look at changes.

compares.title: Nearest whole number vs nearest tenth

watch_out.wrong: 6.95 is 7 when rounded to the nearest whole number and 6.9 when rounded to the nearest tenth.
watch_out.right: 6.95 rounds to 7.0 to the nearest tenth, because the hundredths digit 5 rounds up (p.17).

worked.title: Worked example 2 — round to the nearest tenth
worked.problem: Round 8.80, 6.45 and 3.95 to the nearest tenth.
steps: Look at the hundredths digit of each number: 0, 5 and 5.
0 is in 0–4, so 8.80 rounds down and the tenths digit stays 8.
5 is in 5–9, so 6.45 rounds up to 6.5 and 3.95 rounds up, carrying into the ones to give 4.0.
Keep one decimal place in every answer.
worked.why: 3.95 shows why the carry matters: rounding the tenths digit up from 9 changes the whole number too.

flashcards.front_en: Name the three places after the decimal point.
flashcards.back_en: Tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

flashcards.front_en: What happens to the digits when you multiply by 1000?
flashcards.back_en: Every digit moves three places to the left.

flashcards.front_en: What happens to the digits when you divide by 100?
flashcards.back_en: Every digit moves two places to the right.

flashcards.front_en: Rounding to the nearest tenth: which digit do you look at?
flashcards.back_en: The hundredths digit. 0–4 rounds down, 5–9 rounds up.

flashcards.front_en: Rounding to the nearest whole number: which digit do you look at?
flashcards.back_en: The tenths digit, using the same 0–4 down, 5–9 up rule.

flashcards.front_en: How many decimal places has an answer rounded to the nearest tenth?
flashcards.back_en: Always one, even if it is zero.

flashcards.front_en: What does it mean to regroup a number?

quiz.stem_en: What is the value of the digit 7 in 6703.46?
quiz.why_en: The 7 sits in the hundreds column (p.13).

quiz.stem_en: What is the value of the digit 7 in 213.807?
quiz.why_en: It is the third place after the decimal point (p.13).

quiz.stem_en: What is the value of the digit 7 in 456.702?
quiz.why_en: It is the first place after the decimal point (p.13).

quiz.stem_en: What does the digit 5 in 3.065 represent?
quiz.why_en: It is the third place after the decimal point (WB p.9).

quiz.stem_en: How many times bigger is the value of the digit 6 in 64.53 than the value of the digit 6 in 0.367?
quiz.why_en: 6 tens against 6 hundredths is three places, so 1000 times (p.19).

quiz.stem_en: In the number 13.136, which digit is in the hundredths place?
quiz.why_en: Hundredths is the second place after the decimal point (p.13).

quiz.stem_en: What is 5.6 × 100?
quiz.why_en: Every digit moves two places to the left (WB p.11).
Every digit moves three places to the left (WB p.11).

quiz.stem_en: What is 670 ÷ 1000?
quiz.why_en: Every digit moves three places to the right (WB p.11).

quiz.stem_en: What is 191 ÷ 100?
quiz.why_en: Every digit moves two places to the right (WB p.11).

quiz.stem_en: Find the missing number: ___ × 0.9 = 9
quiz.why_en: 0.9 must move one place to the left, so multiply by 10 (p.19).

quiz.stem_en: Find the missing number: 705 ÷ ___ = 7.05
quiz.why_en: The digits move two places to the right, so divide by 100 (p.19).

quiz.stem_en: A number is multiplied by 10, then by 10 again, then by 10 again, and the answer is 7. What was the starting number?
quiz.why_en: Three multiplications by 10 is × 1000, so reverse it: 7 ÷ 1000 (WB p.12).

quiz.stem_en: Write 10 + 3 + 1 tenth + 3 hundredths + 6 thousandths as a decimal number.
quiz.why_en: Each part goes in its own place value column (p.13).

quiz.stem_en: Copy and complete: 87.655 = 80 + 7 + ___
quiz.why_en: The decimal part decomposes into 6 tenths, 5 hundredths and 5 thousandths (p.19).

quiz.stem_en: What decimal number is 90 + 7 + 3 tenths + 1 hundredth + 4 thousandths?
quiz.why_en: Put each part in its place value column (p.19).

quiz.stem_en: Magda regroups 56.079. Which of these is NOT the same number?
quiz.why_en: 56 + 0.79 is 56.79, which is ten times bigger in the decimal part (WB p.9).

quiz.stem_en: Which expression is equal to 4.063?
quiz.why_en: 6 is in the hundredths place and 3 in the thousandths place (WB p.11).

quiz.stem_en: Why do we round numbers?

choices.en: To make them easier to describe and understand

quiz.why_en: Rounding makes numbers easier to describe and understand (p.16).

quiz.stem_en: What is 4.09 rounded to the nearest whole number?
quiz.why_en: The tenths digit is 0, so round down (p.16).

quiz.stem_en: What is 7.45 rounded to the nearest whole number?
quiz.why_en: The tenths digit is 4, which is in 0–4, so round down (p.16).

quiz.stem_en: A book costs $14.65. What is that to the nearest dollar?
quiz.why_en: The tenths digit is 6, so round up (p.16).

quiz.stem_en: What is 9.55 rounded to the nearest whole number?
quiz.why_en: The tenths digit is 5, so round up from 9 to 10 (p.19).

quiz.stem_en: What is 8.80 rounded to the nearest tenth?
quiz.why_en: The hundredths digit is 0, so round down (p.16).

quiz.stem_en: What is 3.95 rounded to the nearest tenth?
quiz.why_en: The hundredths digit 5 rounds the tenths digit up from 9, carrying into the ones (p.16).

quiz.stem_en: What is 3.08 rounded to the nearest tenth?
quiz.why_en: The hundredths digit is 8, so round up (p.19).

quiz.stem_en: What is 9.07 rounded to the nearest tenth?
quiz.why_en: The hundredths digit is 7, so round up (p.17).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these rounds to 7.5 to the nearest tenth?
quiz.why_en: 7.49 has hundredths digit 9, so the 4 tenths round up to 5 (p.17).

quiz.stem_en: Rounded to the nearest tenth, how many decimal places must the answer always have?

choices.en: Exactly one, even if it is zero
As many as the original number

quiz.why_en: There must always be one decimal place in the answer (p.16).

quiz.stem_en: Is this true: 3.04 is 3 to the nearest whole number and 3 to the nearest tenth?

choices.en: No — to the nearest tenth it is 3.0
No, to the nearest whole number it is 4

quiz.why_en: A number rounded to the nearest tenth keeps one decimal place (p.17).
